Sapara Monastery

An active monastery hidden on a cliff terrace near Akhaltsikhe, with 13th-century frescoes.

Time needed
2 h
From Tbilisi
215 km · 3:35
Road
Mostly paved
Car needed
Crossover / SUV
Season
All year
Entry
free

Sapara stands southeast of Akhaltsikhe at the end of a tight valley, built onto a terrace in the cliff face. The location was chosen so that the monastery is almost invisible from below — the name itself means hidden. That concealment is largely why it survived while other monasteries of Meskheti were destroyed.

A community existed here by the 9th or 10th century, but Sapara flourished under the Jaqeli princes. At the end of the 13th century Beka Jaqeli built the main church of St Saba, which remains the centre of the complex. Its walls carry painting from the same period, one of the significant surviving examples of medieval Georgian wall art.

Altogether the site holds around a dozen churches and chapels, a bell tower, monastic quarters and partly preserved defensive walls. It is an active monastery with a permanent community of monks.

Worth focusing on:

  • the frescoes of St Saba's church and the painted sanctuary
  • the view down the valley from the edge of the terrace
  • the quiet, which unlike at Vardzia is genuine — coaches rarely make the climb

Sapara is only half an hour from Akhaltsikhe and pairs naturally with a visit to Rabati Castle on the same day.

Practical advice

This is a working monastery: women need a headscarf and a long skirt, men long trousers, and shorts will not get you in. Photography inside the churches is normally not permitted. Come in the morning or mid-afternoon, and keep quiet during services. Leave the car on the small terrace below the complex and walk the last stretch up. Toilets are basic; there is no cafe and no ATM, with the nearest in Akhaltsikhe about thirty kilometres back.

How to get there from Tbilisi

From Tbilisi take the usual road to Khashuri, then Borjomi and Akhaltsikhe — roughly 215 km and three and a half hours. From Akhaltsikhe turn southeast; the final eight or nine kilometres are a narrow, steep serpentine. Asphalt exists but has collapsed in places, and two cars barely pass each other on the bends, which is why a crossover is the better choice. After rain or in winter this section becomes noticeably harder. Fill up in Akhaltsikhe, because there is nothing at all above the town.
